extracted.intended_audience: general readers / travelers interested in 19th-century Buenos Ayres social customs
extracted.subtask_description: Excerpt from a 19th-century travelogue describing social etiquette, dress, amusements, domestic arrangements, and legal/social practices in Buenos Ayres for general readers and travelers. The text records normative statements about proper behaviour, customs, and local institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female public arm-taking etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: When walking in public, the female rarely takes the arm of a gentleman, except at night; with married persons this is more common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting a gentleman's arm in daylight is considered unsocial; at dark the restriction ceases. Offering one's arm to accompany a lady for a few streets in daytime would be 'the height of vulgarity' according to local manners; English notions of gentility differ.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escort and visiting norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentlemen escort ladies mainly to the theatre or public places; visits and shopping are usually done in the company of their own sex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a lady allows a gentleman to proceed beside her briefly in the street, it is improper for him to offer his arm. Social conventions restrict mixed-company walking and accompaniment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ballroom and dance solicitation etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: At balls, females sit together when not dancing; gentlemen approach with hesitating steps to solicit a lady to dance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gentlemen's approach while ladies rest is tentative and formal; the social ritual governs who solicits and when.

rubrics_metrics.name: General Spanish respect toward females
rubrics_metrics.description: Spaniards pride themselves upon the delicacy and respect with which they treat females.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author hopes this respect will endure despite other customs 'more honoured in the breach than the observance.' This functions as a local standard of behaviour toward women.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family dancing as multigenerational pastime
rubrics_metrics.description: Evening hours and family dances are common; daughters, mothers, and grandmothers dance together with spirit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These family dances demonstrate that age need not mean moroseness; strangers may be invited into homes with the compliment that the family is 'entirely at your service.' Such invitations are genuine social hospitality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Musical education expectation for young ladies
rubrics_metrics.description: The piano-forte is the favourite instrument and every well-educated young lady is supposed to possess some knowledge of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good performance and instruction are valued; English instruments and makers (Clementi, Stodart) are preferred; male teachers and English female instructors find employment. Public trials of musical skill (show-offs) occur occasionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental supervision and chaperoning of daughters
rubrics_metrics.description: Mothers keep a sharp look-out after their daughters, attending them to public places and in the streets; absent mothers delegate care to slaves or servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strict supervision before marriage is common; some mothers watch with austerity. The text cautions that slaves can be bribed and reports of lovers using slaves to convey messages exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevalence of early marriage and naming customs
rubrics_metrics.description: Marriage often takes place at an early age (frequently at thirteen and fourteen); married females preserve their maiden name conjoined with their husband's surname; children bear the father's surname and often receive a Christian name based on their saint's day.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Women 'ripen into womanhood' sooner and beauties fade earlier compared with England. The saint-day naming custom makes name selection effectively a lottery across classes; some romantic names are common.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family cohabitation after marriage
rubrics_metrics.description: Custom of all the family living together after marriage is common and may seem strange to English ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While English readers may expect petty jealousies, local custom and temperament mitigate quarrels; the author admires the happiness this arrangement can produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Christian name and honorifics in address
rubrics_metrics.description: When speaking or writing to an individual, the Spanish custom is to use the Christian name with honorifics (Don/Doña) instead of the surname.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This form of address ('Don Carlos', 'Doña Dominga') is considered pleasing and more romantic than English 'Mr. Smith' styles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of respectable families performing domestic work
rubrics_metrics.description: Respectable families do not consider it disgraceful to let lodgings, take in washing, and make or mend clothes; slaves perform the labourious parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Domestic occupations are not confined to lower orders as in England. Even wives of local magistrates may take needle-work; such practices reflect local social norms rather than scandal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washerwomen practices and spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: Washerwomen perform washing on the beach in long lines extending nearly two miles; they dry linen on the ground and celebrate joyous occasions with African-style ceremonies, dances, and music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Robberies among washerwomen are punished by ducking. Their adherence to African customs is notable; at the approach of rain confusion is great as they rush to save linen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal status of slavery (abolition and residual slavery)
rubrics_metrics.description: Slavery was abolished in 1810; those born prior to that time remain slaves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slaves can demand their 'paper' (the deed binding them) and seek other employers; they can allege cruelty to the alcalde. For serious misbehaviour owners can punish by flogging; there are other chastisements for females. The text notes humane treatment in Buenos Ayres compared with other countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treatment and social position of slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Female slaves are often placed more on the footing of friends than mere servants; they attend their mistresses, sit in the chamber at needle-work, and imitate fashionable society; men slaves when deserving are treated kindly too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author praises humane treatment and notes that kind behaviour tends to produce affectionate and grateful slaves; some discontent exists but is exceptional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public order and civility in streets
rubrics_metrics.description: Lower orders in the streets exhibit excellent and orderly conduct compared with other countries; obscene insults and molestation of modest females are rare.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This civility contributes to a foreigner's sense of safety. The author contrasts this with English lower-order rowdiness, noting he would not curtail liberty to buy civility but would welcome some moderation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drunkenness prevalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Drunkenness is not a general vice of the country, although some rabble of blacks and porters may be occasionally drunk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mechanics employ spare hours with guitar, singing, dancing, and smoking rather than seeking public-house grog as in England.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begging etiquette / method to repel beggars
rubrics_metrics.description: Beggars besiege courtyards and streets; the best way to get rid of them is to exclaim 'Perdone por Dios!' (pardon for God's sake).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This phrase is effective locally but would be less so among European beggars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bathing customs and decency norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Bathing in summer by all classes, particularly ladies, is fashionable; they bathe at the front of town without bathing machines, attended by female slaves, using bathing clothes and managing undressing/dressing discreetly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because it is customary and circumspect, foreign criticisms of indecency are judged unfair. Many lanterns are lit at night; bathing machines would be an improvement because swimmers must walk a quarter mile to deep water and bottoms are stony. Not respectable persons venture near bathing areas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Male dress norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Gentlemen of Buenos Ayres follow English fashion with adaptations for heat: jackets and light trousers, straw hats (including Chili shapes); jackets are not considered genteel at the theatre or parties; in summer light clothing prevails.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boys' dress also mirrors adult men's attire (long coats, capotes, large hats), making children resemble little adults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Female dress and grooming standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Female street dress is enchanting and similar to ball-room dress; white prevails, shawls serve as veil and covering, waists are of intermediate length, frocks/petticoats are short to display ankles and feet, tight shoes are common, hair is grown long and worn with combs and ringlets, caps/bonnets are not worn even in old age, and fans are constant companions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many change dress multiple times daily; attention to hair is great and powder/disguises to hide age are not used. Mourning does not continue as long as in England; children dress similarly to adults. Tight shoes often cause limping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attitude toward mourning and widow dress
rubrics_metrics.description: Wearing of mourning does not continue as long as in England; young and handsome widows are not disfigured by close melancholic caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author expresses aesthetic approval of the local costume (basquina) and less severe mourning practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Travel modes and carriage norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Not many carriages or coaches exist, but they are increasing; the calle coche is much used (drawn by two horses or mules, passengers seated sideways); family travelling uses heavy Spanish-style carriages with mules and many attendants; persons mostly go on horseback for expedition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carriages are expensive and slow but save fatigue; Morris the coach-maker profits due to scarcity of good carriages; travelling to the Andes takes about fourteen days on horseback, crossing to Santiago about three weeks at full gallop.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horse ownership, care, and market norms
rubrics_metrics.description: Horses range from 3 to 100 dollars; very good ones about 17 dollars; average 12–13 hands high, long tails, endure much fatigue; keep is dear (12–17 dollars/month); hay not much used; grass carts supply feed daily.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: English breeds may not thrive due to climate; comfortable stabling and grooming are uncommon because horses are cheap and plentiful. Every horse has a burnt mark to trace ownership; theft has declined with police regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Riding equipment and riding style
rubrics_metrics.description: English saddles are in vogue, but the local 'ricado' saddle (serves as saddle and bed) and Spanish bridle/bit are preferred; stirrups are long and considered graceful; ladies ride but handle horses less dexterously; lower orders ride odd-legged with one toe in stirrup and gallop for miles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Galloping in town is not permitted; the country waggons and harness methods differ from English practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Popular sports and amusements
rubrics_metrics.description: Sports and amusements include horse-races near the Recolator (natives ride without saddle), cock-fighting (valued, English game-cocks fetch thirty to forty dollars), shooting (birds abundant), and an annual fair beginning October 12th with booths, swings, military band, dancing, and guitar music.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hunting with greyhounds/foxhounds is poor due to lack of foxes; shooting and bird sport suit English sportsmen; fishing is uncommon as a sport and often performed on horseback using nets hauled by horses; the annual fair and carnival are important social events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gambling customs and enforcement
rubrics_metrics.description: A propensity to gaming exists, especially among males; no public gaming houses (government discourages them), but gambling occurs privately; police intervene and take principals rather than arrest large groups.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Englishmen participate; even boys (milk-boys) gamble and sometimes lose daily receipts. The text compares some local gamblers favorably (in skill) with English examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Carnival water-throwing custom and its risks
rubrics_metrics.description: During Carnival, people amuse themselves by throwing buckets and pans of water from rooftops and windows, and egg-shells filled with water are sold and used to soak passers-by; the practice lasts three days and many go out of town to avoid it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice has led to serious illness for some; newspapers and police have attempted to suppress it with limited effect; participants (including ladies and strangers) take active part; visitors unfamiliar with custom may react angrily.
